The House resumed from Wednesday, November 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lewis that Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate. This is a critically important issue, an issue which we as legislators I am sure have all had to struggle with. How can I discuss abortion when this is really not an abortion bill? This government has brought in legislation, Bill C-43, which it hopes will address these problems. Bill C-43 does not address the problems, Bill C-43 certainly does not correct the problems, and Bill C-43 fails the fundamental test. Therefore it must not be passed.
Let me deal with some of the arguments I have been hearing from both sides. The first argument is that at least now we have some legislation, inadequate as it is. It is better than having no legislation which of course is the equivalent of abortion on demand.
Let us pass this bill and get it into committee where we can make some changes. We should draft the amendments. We should approve them and incorporate them into the legislation. However, before it receives Royal Assent, we should send it to the Supreme Court on a reference to test it against the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
It is the duty of the governing party to bring forth legislation. It is also the duty of the Opposition to challenge, correct and refine this legislation. It is also the duty of this House, then, to pass or reject the proposed law. It is also the duty of Parliament to legislate. What this government has done is bring forth a neutral proposal without substance.
The proposed new abortion law has as its overriding objective the balance of interests, the rights and interests of women and society's interest, in the protection of the foetus. This legislation does not realize this objective. This legislation really satisfies no one, not those who
oppose the termination of pregnancy or those who prefer choice as to whether or not to terminate a pregnancy.
The proposed legislation is contrary to this decision. It invites any third party to press criminal charges against a doctor or a woman if there is evidence that an unlawful early termination was performed; that is, an abortion that was performed without first ensuring it was in the best interest of the woman's psychological, mental or physical health.
The question of the rights of the unborn child also must be addressed. This legislation does not address this issue. If you will remember Joseph Borowski failed to assert foetal rights because there was no longer an abortion law upon which to base a challenge. The proposed legislation does not address the rights of the unborn child. As we discuss the rights of the unborn, let us attempt to remove God or religion from the argument for a moment. If we remove this from the equation, the greatest thing still left to us is life.
Even the most radical secular person, the most hedonistic person in the world, must struggle with the fundamental questions of when life begins, when life ends, under what circumstances life can be ended and when life must be protected. What authority protects this life? Is it legal? Is it medical? Is it the church, or is it a combination of all these elements?
As a society, what protection do we extend to the lives of the helpless? What protection do we extend to the lives of the dying? What protection do we extend to the aged? Better still, what protection do we extend to the life of the unborn? We must look at life in all of its phases.
At the very least, even if some scientist or theologian states that in the early stages we cannot discern human life, the full potential of human life is indisputably there. That to my mind on its own should demand some respect and caution. At the very least, the potential for life exists and should unequivocally be respected.
I think all you have to do is visit your aged mother or grandmother and kiss her tenderly or give your spouse or your friend a warm hug, take a child's hand or let an infant grasp your finger and look into his eyes, all the time remembering that the only difference between the very oldest and the very youngest is only time. Their humanity has not changed.
November 23, 1989

This legislation is about life but fails to deal with life. This legislation is deficient. Providing the doctor will accept the reasons concerning the health of the female person, physical, mental or psychological, the doctor can terminate the pregnancy.
A doctor can terminate the pregnancy from the moment of conception to the moment prior to birth. That is what this bill implies. There are no guidelines; there are no rules. This government has evaded its responsibility and shifted the onus to the medical community.
As a layman I have great difficulty understanding the medical community. On the one hand we see premature births using every available means to sustain life, the doctors using every new advancement without questions of cost to save the life of a premature child. In the same instance, perhaps in the very same hospital, they are terminating the life of an unborn child. Moreover, to augment the deficiencies in this bill, there is no precise definition of the health reasons that would allow the termination of a pregnancy.
This legislation attempts to many two incompatible positions: that abortion should be illegal and punishable by imprisonment while at the same time available to all Canadian women based on the value judgment of the physician. There is no development of the concept of the unborn child, no requirement that the unborn child has rights which must be respected. This bill fails in this respect.
I listened with interest a couple of days ago to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development who both have diametrically opposed views, yet they both said they can support this legislation; another inconsistency from the very people who proposed Bill C-43.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this morning to speak to Bill C-43. I will divide my speech into two sections. First, I will consider this legislation in my capacity as elected repre-
Govemment Orders
sentative of the residents of the vast riding of Charlesbourg and as a legislator here in the House of Commons, and second, as a woman and mother who believes that family and children are part of the fundamental values of our society.
When I look at the positions that have developed among the people of my riding, I realize they are not much different from those taken by Canadians as a whole. There are people who are stubbornly pro life and pro choice, but most of the representations I received contained a request that the federal government act responsibly and fill the legal vacuum created by the Supreme Court's judgment in January 1988.
In the spring of that year, those of us who were sitting in the House will remember the splits that developed among members when a motion proposing three legislative options was tabled in the House for debate. Although it was to be a free vote, and despite the fact that the debate was long and intense, it was impossible to reach a consensus on one of the three options or on any of the many amendments that were presented.
At the end of this debate, many members believed that new abortion legislation would no longer be necessary. They were soon forced to reconsider that position, however. This summer, day after day, Canadians were headed to what I would call a macabre expose of very personal problems on the front pages of our information media. This public airing causes people in my riding to reconsider their position and that the government should intervene to give this country legislation that would not be too permissive but that would nevertheless reflect Canadian realities in this respect.
Bill C-43 before the House today was not the result of a mere whim. It represents many hours of study, consultation and analysis to ensure that the proposed legislation reflects the benchmark established by the Supreme Court and based on the dictates of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Mr. Speaker, what strikes me in this Bill is that it recognises the health aspect. It also acknowledges that the decision is up to the woman and her doctor. Furthermore, the bill's objective is to balance the constitutional rights of women and society's interest in the protection of the foetus.

November 23, 1989
Government Orders
All these measures lead me to believe that the new legislation will pass the test of the Supreme Court, that a consensus will be reached in this House and that the bill will become Canada's new legislation in this area.
In a debate that is often emotionally charged, I must say that as a woman and a mother of four children, it is much harder to put one's personal convictions into perspective. Of course, I do not think abortion is necessarily the only solution. I believe that abortion should always be considered as a last resort and that women should have access to all the support they need to make such a difficult decision. It is easy to talk about abortion, whether we are pro-choice or pro-life, and it is easy to make decisions for others in hypothetical situations. One has to experience these situations, however, to realize that making this kind of decision is extremely difficult and that at this point, we need people who can give advice.
If I were to comment on the suggestions made by my colleague at National Health and Welfare, for instance, I think I would have to say that it is extremely important to ensure that all cases come before a doctor. I also think that we must have in the community people who have certain values and are able to provide advice, help and support.
Sometimes when I see demonstrations by people who are solidly pro-life, I wonder whether it would not be more useful to channel all that energy in to giving support to the people who need it.
I think that our society needs more compassion and more love, and that these fundamental values are essential if we are to make any kind of progress. People in these circumstances are often in financial difficulty, they need help and they should be given that help.
When I look at the bill, I think we have achieved a certain balance, and I must say that as a Member of the House of Commons and as a woman, I agree with the proposed measures and I intend to vote for Bill C-43 on second reading.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak on this debate for a few minutes this morning because the debate taking place in the House over the last few days is perhaps one of the
most important in terms of human values that we will have in this Parliament for some time to come.
The preamble of the Constitution of this nation states that Canada was founded on principles recognizing the supremacy of God and the rule of the law. I accept those principles, but I further believe in the sanctity of human life, and I will work and fight to protect the rights of unborn children.
The law, however, that was intended to provide protection to the unborn was struck down on January 28, 1988, but interestingly enough not by a unanimous decision of the court. Since Parliament is the only body that can enact legislation to protect the lives of unborn children, we as elected members of this institution have a responsibility to bring forward a law that is workable and practical but at the same time protects unborn children.
The recent voter survey conducted by one of our colleagues in the other place reveals that 59 per cent of Canadians were not aware that there were one million abortions approved in Canada since 1969. Most of those were paid for by medicare. Yet 66 per cent of those surveyed believed that life begins at conception, while 73 per cent of those considered an unborn child at any stage a human being.
If we then consider the results of the survey, first that life begins at conception, that an unborn child at any stage is a human being, then of course the current status of this issue is nothing more than a wanton disregard for human life.
The medical legal protection of foetal life dates back to the Oath Of Hippocrates, 460 to 377 BC, which predates the birth of Christ. This oath states: "I will give neither a deadly drug to anyone who has asked for it, nor will I make a suggestion to this effect. Similarly, I will not give to a woman an abortion remedy". I have to suggest to this House today that if this proposed legislation, Bill C-43, goes through, it flies directly in conflict with that Oath of Hippocrates.
The letters I have received on this issue are running 50 to 1 against abortion, but there are three in particular that stand out above all others. These are from doctors in my constituency. I want to read excerpts from them into the record today. I quote the first doctor:
I would encourage the defeat of this legislation in order to obtain
more effective legislation which will protect the rights of the unborn
child and ultimately the health of the mother. There is conclusive
November 23, 1989

evidence that the action of abortion has serious health consequences on the mother as well, and we need to give consideration to their wellbeing also.
Another letter states:
The government which fails to protect the lives of the people within its care, no matter how young or old, is a moral failure. The institution has been established to assume some degree of moral authority. The Canadian government demonstrates this in regard to many human rights by making laws against murder, assault, racism, et cetera, and by promoting equality for all Canadians. Is a request for the protection of life too much to ask of one's own government?
The third letter states:
I am writing to express my concern over the lack of protection in Canadian law for the life of unborn children. Abortion at any stage of pregnancy is the deliberate killing of an innocent human being. To say that this is a woman's right to have control over her own body totally ignores the reality of fact that there are two or more lives involved in a pregnancy. A woman has legal rights over her own body but she (and all society) has a moral obligation to protect the helpless being in her womb.
At this time we are seeing the tragic spectacle of women -fighting through the courts to have her unborn child destroyed although she is now at the stage of pregnancy when the child, if born, could probably be saved.
Other abortions differ only in that the baby generally would have no chance of survival.
I urge you to fight in the House of Commons for a law giving total protection to the unborn.
These three doctors-two of them are family doctors from my constituency-who took the time to write on this issue before us today have said it all and probably much more eloquently than I did. Their depth of knowledge, their respect for human life and their moral principles must reflect the feelings of thousands of Canadians across this nation.
When we examine this bill before the House today, we find that it really creates no legally imposed delays or obstruction to obtaining a legal abortion other than the necessity to consult with other doctors. Of course, if the first doctor does not agree, you would go on to others, hoping that you would find one who would. In fact, this bill as it sits before this Parliament today is not far from being abortion on demand.
I fully realize that this bill is at second reading debate and that debate is on the principle of this bill. Therefore, in the parliamentary process it will go on to committee, to report stage and then on to third reading. I want to call on the government at this point either to bring forward amendments or to be receptive to amendments
Government Orders
of members of this House that will provide protection to unborn children.
As I indicated earlier, there are two or more lives involved in a pregnancy. While I clearly accept the exceptions to save the life of the mother, this bill does very little to save the lives of unborn children. At this point in the debate I believe that I would be remiss if I did not remind members of the House that it is stated in the preamble to our Constitution that we believe as Canadians in the supremacy of God.
The Bible itself mentions repeatedly-and it is on this Bible that we as members took our oaths-in Genesis 4:1, Jeremiah 1:5 and Job 33:4, children in the womb. A child conceived in the womb develops in the womb and is bom from the womb.
Therefore, if we accept the supremacy of God as stated in the preamble to the Constitution, then we in turn have an obligation to accept the teachings of the Bible. Consequently, we must also accept the fact that a foetus is a child or a human being and as such this nation has a duty to protect unborn children, to preserve their right to be bom and to enjoy the rights and obligations of human beings.
As those of us in this House realize, those of us who are older, life itself takes on a new meaning. I as a farmer never cease going out in the spring of the year to the fields and the pastures. Life is all about us. We see the birds, the animals, the new growth, the trees, the grass and the flowers. There is a sense of nearness to one's Creator, our Creator who said: "Suffer the little children to be brought unto me."
This debate is about human life. We are debating human life, the lives of unborn children, and I ask members of this House to consider the lives of these unborn children above all else.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to reaffirm and to expand on remarks I made in this House on this topic last year.
After that court decision in the Morgentaler case I canvassed my constituents to seek their opinion as to three possible courses of action. The first would be to permit abortion only when the mother's life or physical health was in danger. The second would permit abortion without restriction. The third choice would permit abortion without restriction during the first 16 weeks and

Government Orders
thereafter, only where the mother's life or physical health was in danger.
Some 64 per cent chose option one; 9 per cent, option 2; and 24 per cent, option 3. The clear majority of the people in my riding believes that abortion should be allowed only if the mother's life or physical health is endangered. Indeed more women respondents than men supported that position.
It happens that I agree with the majority of my constituents, but even if I did not I believe that where there is a clear expression of opinion within a constituency and, in the absence of party discipline, a member ought to respect the wishes of his constituents.
As a Christian and one whose personal philosophy is respect for the basic worth of the individual, the sanctity of human life and the primacy of the family in our society, I believe that, in so far as is possible, every human life from conception should be given a chance.
This latest chapter in the abortion debate began in January of last year when the Supreme Court in the Morgantaler case struck down Section 251 of the Criminal Code on the grounds that the procedures deprived the pregnant woman of the right to security of her person under Section 7 of the Charter. Since that time Canada has been without a law.
The government attempted to fill the void in July 1988 with a compromise resolution based on the gestational approach. This proposal along with five others ranging all the way from classic pro-life to pro-choice was debated and voted on, all six questions were defeated in this House, and Canada was left without a law.
In March 1989 the Supreme Court rejected the Bo-rowski appeal because Section 251 had already been struck down. When the judges refused to rule on the rights of the unborn in the abstract, they indicated again that it was up to the legislature to make law.
Then came the Dodds and Daigle cases in the summer of 1989. The media spectacle accompanying these cases made it obvious that we could not continue to live in a state of lawlessness. It is up to the federal government to exercise leadership in filling this void.
The division of legislative powers under our Constitution is such that the only area under which the federal government has the appropriate authority is the criminal law. If this issue is not dealt with under the criminal law, then it must devolve to the provinces with the prospect of more chaos. Consequently, the government has brought forward this compromise, Bill C-43.
Last week the Supreme Court in the Daigle v. Tremblay case noted that the courts have consistently concluded that to enjoy rights the foetus must be bom alive. The court went on to address the matter of a potential father's rights and concluded "that no court in Quebec or elsewhere had ever accepted the argument that a father's interest in the foetus which he helped to create could support a right to veto a woman's decision in respect to the foetus she was carrying."
In short, the courts are saying that for a foetus to enjoy certain rights before birth or for a potential father to exercise any possible rights, there must be substantive legal reasons. There must be legislation-a decision taken by legislators based on social, political, economic, and moral choices.
Here we are again in November 1989 revisiting this issue, an issue which Parliament failed to resolve in six free votes in the summer of 1988, an issue which the courts have clearly indicated belongs to the people of Canada as expressed through their elected representatives, an issue on which Canadians in all walks of life are divided, an issue on which individual Canadians are sincerely and honestly at odds with each other.
It is important that all Canadians understand the procedure involved in dealing with Bill C-43 which the government has proposed as a compromise to end the current state of lawlessness. Bill C-43 makes it an offence to induce an abortion unless the procedure is done by or under the direction of a medical practitioner who is of the opinion that if the abortion were not induced the health or life of the female person would likely be threatened.
We are currently debating this bill at second reading. Under the rules of this House no substantive amendments as to the content of the bill are allowed at this stage. Members will vote yes or no. If they vote no, the bill fails and we revert to a legislative void. If the answer is yes, then the bill goes to a legislative committee composed of 15 members from all sides.
November 23, 1989

The legislative committee can hear witnesses, receive submissions, propose and vote on amendments, and then report the bill back to the House where it will be voted on. This is called report stage. At report stage members other than those on the legislative committee can also propose amendments. Obviously there will be amendments and there will be opportunities for members to vote on these amendments at report stage.
At the final stage, third reading, there will be further debate and an opportunity to vote for or against the finished product. Bill C-43 does recriminalize abortion. Bill C-43 does reject the gestational approach. Bill C-43 presents a health standard in determining grounds for ending unborn life. That is important because if the day ever comes when we as a society arbitrarily measure the value of life by its stages, we are on a very slippery slope.
Bill C-43 is opposed by pro-choice people who want no law at all. It is equally opposed by pro-life advocates who would restrict abortion further. Indeed one such pro-life advocate said to me that this bill is worthless, it would be better to have no law at all. With respect, I disagree. It is the pro-choice advocates who want no law. It is the New Democratic Party that wants unrestricted access to abortion. I cannot and will not support that position.
Therefore I intend to support this bill on second reading in order to get it to the legislative committee. This will allow for witnesses and for amendments and for the possibility of changes which might improve the bill. I believe it would be wrong to defeat the bill at this stage. To do so would not only deny the opportunity to work on the bill and to improve it but would also return the nation to a state of lawlessness.
Clearly we must have a law. We have laws to regulate the speed of vehicles and where they can park. Surely it is not too much to ask for a statement as to the validity of life itself, a law that reflects our beliefs, that a living being is involved and that life has value regardless of its stage of development. If it is easy and straightforward and acceptable to terminate life near its beginning, then is it any great leap forward towards ending life at other stages in circumstances where there may be inconve-
Govemment Orders
nience or cost? What comfort will there be for the elderly, the handicapped, the sick and, ultimately, for those who see things differently from those in power?
What is it that separates our society from past totalitarian regimes? Surely one characteristic is that of reverence and respect for life, whether at the beginning or near the end or indeed at any stage.
In closing I want to touch on a couple of peripheral issues. One relates to demographics. Declining birth rates and population trends indicate that Canada will not be able to sustain its present population, let alone increase it, without immigration. By the year 2015, if present trends continue, there will be almost as many Canadians 55 years of age and over as there will be in the 25 to 54 age group. This projection raises serious questions about our ability to pay for pensions or medicare or care for an aging population. Ironically, every statistic points to the need for a policy to promote and encourage a higher birth rate in this country.
I do applaud the establishment of a royal commission to examine the implications of the new technology available to human reproduction as well as the economic ramifications thereof. I would have preferred that the mandate be widened to encompass not just the host of questions surrounding reproductive technology but also those of euthanasia, suicide and all issues of intentional intervention in the human life cycle. The sanctity of human life runs through all of these issues.
Finally, I want to commend members on all sides for their participation in this debate. I have listened intently to their positions, some quite opposed to mine, but all sincere and all reflecting the profound challenge before us; to address an issue in which the views of virtually every individual Canadian differ in some degree, some irreconcilably.
Members of Parliament can do only that which is possible. Sometimes, indeed most of the time, we arrive at compromises. The result may not be what we would have preferred as individuals but it is the best that we can do collectively. Whatever happens, there must be every effort made to assist and improve adoptive processes. Whatever happens, we must encourage efforts toward greater understanding, heightened awareness and, most important of all, individual responsibility.

November 23, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak against this bill. The reason I am speaking against it is that while it appears to support the prochoice position that insists that the question of abortion is a matter between a woman and her doctor, in fact it is exactly the same position that was taken in the previous abortion legislation which was overturned by the Supreme Court. This legislation leaves the decision not up to the woman but up to the doctor. A woman may attempt to choose a doctor that supports her viewpoint on abortion but, in fact, the doctor has the final decision on whether that woman should carry a foetus to term or should have an abortion. That is precisely the question that the Supreme Court dealt with in Morgentaler and struck down.
Essentially it is a repeat of the legislation that we had a few years ago where the government set up in the Criminal Code a therapeutic abortion committee that was appointed by hospitals which performed abortions. What this legislation does is reduce the number of people on that committee from three to one. It still leaves the decision as to whether an abortion can be performed up to the doctor rather than the woman herself. That is the problem with this legislation and that is the reason why I intend to vote against it.
This legislation, in my view, is anachronistic and atavistic. It is based on the idea that the reproduction functions of a woman have a third party interest in them. In the past the husband or the father saw the woman as a chattel, as a piece of personal property. Our laws considered a woman to be a chattel of her husband or father. In a modem pluralistic society which recognizes the rights of all individuals, this type of primitive, atavistic belief simply cannot prevail and I am surprised that it is being restated in this legislation.
The decision with respect to abortion should be a decision solely of the woman in consultation with any doctor, medical person or other authority that she chooses to consult. I must reiterate that the decision itself should remain with the woman involved and not with the doctor.
As I said, there was a time not long ago when we considered in our legislation and in our society that women where the chattels of their fathers until such
time as they became the chattels of their husbands. It has only been within the last seven decades that women have had a right to vote in this country, to exercise the same right in politics that males in our society have exercised for hundreds of years. Women have only had the right to vote for the past seven decades.
It has only been within the past four or five decades that women have been considered persons with respect to their rights before the law. Our society has not advanced very far from a very primitive view of women, and the legislation that we are debating today is actually a return to that primitive view of women as chattels of their husbands or their fathers. But there is a bit of a difference in this legislation in that the government appears to be nationalizing the interest that the husband or the father had in his chattel and making it an interest of the state in the reproductive functions of women. I do not believe that is a right, proper and democratic thing to do in a society such as ours.
The decision to proceed with an abortion, as other speakers have indicated, is not an easy decision for anyone to make. I can recall when in my family we were looking forward with hope and expectation to the birth of our children. As our children go into high school and university and begin to select a career we continue to look with hope and expectation upon their prospects for the future. It is very enjoyable for parents to be able to do that. But that is not a privilege that all parents in our society enjoy.
To some parents, and especially single parents who are living in poverty or living in difficult circumstances, the possibility of having another child is looked upon with horror. In fact, it is an expectation which causes the family to lose hope for the future and in some cases it is just considered another mouth to feed in a poor family that has difficulty feeding the children they already have. It is an extremely difficult prospect for some of those families to face. Those families feel that in our society they have absolutely no alternative.
The American Medical Association polled all of its members a few years ago and asked what the major medical problems faced by different groups of their patients. The major medical problem facing teenage girls was pregnancy and the second was acne.
November 23, 1989

So it is a serious problem facing children in both Canada and the United States. When we consider that the major concern of teenage girls who go to physicians is pregnancy and the second one is acne, we are dealing with a serious difficulty in this country. When a teenage girl becomes pregnant she does not look on that with the same hope, expectation and excitement with which the rest of us look upon that prospect, she looks at it as something that is going to interfere with her schooling, destroy her career and, in fact, destroy her life as she chooses to live it. It is an extremely difficult prospect for that teenage girl to face.
Doctors are not necessarily all that sympathetic. They may adopt a very narrow view of what constitutes psychological, mental and physical health. That teenage girl will be dependent on the doctor to make a decision as to whether her career is going to be destroyed, whether her school is going to be interrupted, or if she is going to be facing a career which involves poverty, low wage levels and a dead end. So it is a serious problem.
But, in spite of that, no one faces the prospect of having an abortion with anything but extreme concern. As I said, most of us in this room look forward to having children with hope, expectation and excitement, but many people in Canada see it as a terrible prospect which will destroy their future. They look upon abortion in the same way because, having the understanding that the process to create a human life has already been put into effect, no one likes to terminate it, even with all of the terror with which it is anticipated.
This legislation does nothing to help people address that prospect. It does nothing other than give the potential to recriminalize abortion and make the abortion extremely difficult for the women who have to face that prospect.
I find that strange because there are many things that this government could do in order to make abortion the less desirable choice. This is the government that has cut back on assistance to family planning organizations in Canada. This government refuses to fund the availability of birth control information and birth control apparatus to people across Canada.
Government Orders
I think there are three ways that we could reduce abortions in Canada without recriminalizing it. One is to make birth control information and apparatus widely and freely available so that abortion is not an option to be considered. The second is to make access to abortion available to everyone in Canada in the event that that birth control apparatus fails. The third and most important is for this government to reverse its policies and to start supporting families financially and socially so that the prospect of raising children in Canada is not a horrible one of poverty and abuse but one in which you can raise children free of poverty in happy surroundings and with a prospect of a great future. That should be the object of the government's policy to reduce abortions in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on Bill C-43. Abortion is a very difficult issue. Over the last year I have received numerous communications from my constituents. Abortion was raised by many people during the last election campaign as I travelled throughout the riding knocking on doors to encourage people to consider electing me as their member of Parliament. During that process I heard from those who represented a very solid pro-life position. I heard from those who represented a very solid prochoice position. I also heard from those who fell somewhere in between. Consistently I was asked my views on abortion and I was very clear in my position to my constituents on several points. I said that I felt that abortion should not be available on demand and that abortion should not be available simply at the call of an individual, but that I would accept that abortion should be available for specialized circumstances and I had some examples of that.
That answer satisfied neither the pro-life people nor the pro-choice people, but that was my personal feeling. I did say to my constituents that this bill would be a free vote in the House of Commons, as was promised by the Conservative Party, and that I would give my constituents ample opportunity to reflect and to advise me of their wishes as to how I should vote on this issue. I did say to them that I would not necessarily be bound by every specific representation because you can appreciate that if you get 160,000 representations you cannot satisfy them all.
I made the point of meeting with as many people in my constituency as possible and they included the Knights of Columbus in Whitby, various pro-choice people, organizations from Whitby and Ajax, various right-to-life groups from Whitby, Ajax and Pickering and individual

November 23, 1989
Government Orders
citizens. I have an open-door policy in my constituency and if a resident wants to meet with their MP I am available and I will discuss the issues. I do not necessarily need to know in advance what they want to talk about. I had people through my offices who told me in advance that they wanted to discuss abortion and others who simply made appointments and we discussed it while they were there.
I have received many submissions from my constituents on this issue. I did promise my constituents that I would canvass them and learn what they had to say as a group on this particular issue. This I did and I would like to share with you some of the things I learned from them.
In a householder that I sent out early September I asked my constituents many questions on the issue of abortion. They responded with almost 3,300 responses. In fact it was 3,299 at the point when this particular summary was prepared and I think it is probably representative. I have received some additional responses since I prepared these numbers but clearly my constituents have an opinion on the issue of abortion and I would like to share that with members here today and maybe in this way you can appreciate my position on this.
I asked about 17 questions on abortion. The first question I asked was whether the government should pass a law dealing with the issue of abortion. Without asking them to say whether they were for or against or anything else, I asked whey they wanted the government to act on this issue. Eighty-seven per cent of the respondents said yes, and I am happy to say that the government is in fact doing that.
The second question was whether the government should ban abortion outright. The question was very clear, very specific. It said that under no circumstances would an abortion be allowed. My constituents again responded; 19.7 per cent said yes. Of course there is a corollary to that question and that is whether we should legalize abortion on demand for any reason at any time. Thirty-two per cent said yes.
So there you have the view of my constituents. Half of them have said that it is either yes or no completely. The
other half came in with the answers to the balance of the questions.
Because I felt that my constituents should have the opportunity, as I did, to feel that maybe there are some circumstances where an abortion should be available to the individual, I asked a number of questions on that side.
For example, I asked whether my constituents believed that abortion should be available to a victim of rape. Four times as many said yes as said no. Did my constituents believe that abortion should be available to a victim of incest? Four times as many said yes as said no. Should abortion be available when the health of the mother is involved? Sixteen times as many said yes as said no. Should abortion be available if there was proven circumstances that there was a deformity with the foetus? Three times as many said yes as said no.
I also asked various questions relating to the gestational approach because in September, without knowing what the legislation was going to say, it was thought that maybe the legislation would allow abortion based on a gestational approach. I asked my constituents whether abortion should be available in the first eight weeks without question. Eighteen per cent said no, 14 per cent said yes. As to whether it should be available in the first 12 weeks it was 20 per cent no versus 13 per cent yes. At 16 weeks it was 22 per cent no, 9 per cent yes. At 20 weeks it was 24 per cent no. It went all the way up to 28 weeks and it got to 25 per cent no.
Very clearly, as my constituents have indicated by this response, they were not interested in a gestational approach and I note that the bill does not have that. Of course I was not aware that it was not going to be in the bill, but my constituents have clearly indicated to me they did not want me to support a bill that included a gestational approach.
I also asked my constituents whether both parents have the right to input on the decision on an abortion. I do have responses from both males and by females to my survey. I can tell you that they consistently agreed all the way through until I came to this question. More men thought they should have input in the decision of
November 23, 1989

abortion, that both parents should be involved, than did the women. The women very clearly said that it was not the decision of both parents. Although the men felt clearly that it was not both parents' decision, they did feel a little more strongly on this issue.
Family finances was discussed. I asked whether abortion should be available for family finances if there was a problem in that area. Again my constituents said no. I asked whether abortion should be available if the mother was mentally handicapped. The answer was clearly yes.
There was a question about the age of the mother, whether abortion should be available because of the age of the mother. I left the interpretation of that question to the view of the respondent. Clearly they said no, that should not influence the availability of abortion.
Very clearly my constituents have put some rules in place. They have suggested to me that I ought to support some legislation. I can only conclude that this bill in fact does what my constituents have asked me to do. I will be supporting this legislation because I think it goes a long way towards what my constituents have indicated to me very clearly. Personally I might prefer a little more tightness in the bill but I will be supporting this bill because that is what my constituents have indicated they want.
I thank you for the opportunity to present to you the views of my constituents and my personal view on why I will be supporting this legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ten minutes is a very short time to deal with a very complex and difficult question, so I will try to be brief.
I intend to vote in favour of the motion that Bill C-43 be read a second time. I shall do so not because I like this bill in its present form, but because I believe that Canadians abhor the current legislative vacuum. They want legislation that will protect the unborn adequately. They want a law based on the principle that abortion is socially and morally unacceptable as a birth control device.
The bill now before the House is deeply flawed. It is vague and ambiguous in many crucial respects, however the bill gives us a starting point. It can be amended in committee. If we refused even to give this bill second
Government Orders
reading and to send it to a committee, as parliamentarians we may have lost an important opportunity to fill this legislative vacuum. If we throw out this law now, we may be for a long time without a law. So I will vote to allow this bill to go forward to the committee stage. There it can be clarified, strengthened and improved.
I urge the Minister of Justice to give the legislative committee that will consider Bill C-43 ample time to hear expert testimony, to obtain clarification of various provisions and to formulate amendments to improve the bill. I would urge too that the government permit ample time for members on all sides of the House and all sides of this debate to express themselves in this debate and, most importantly, that contrary to common legislative strategy we be given notice well in advance of the timetable for this legislation. Let us not deal with this as a partisan matter.
There will be much for the legislative committee to do. The bill is short but there is much in it that requires clarification. Perhaps the provision subject to the widest scope for interpretation is the portion of subsection (1) of revised Section 287 that makes it not a crime for a medical practitioner to induce an abortion if, in his or her opinion, the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female person would be likely to be threatened.
Subsection (2) proposes for greater certainty that health means physical, mental and psychological health. Also, it defines opinion to be an opinion formed using the generally accepted standards of the medical profession.
In the background information accompanying this bill we are informed by the government that based on majority reasons for judgment in the Morgentaler case, permitting an abortion if the psychological health of the woman is threatened is constitutionally required.
We are also informed in the background information that while the bill does not specifically refer to eugenics, rape, incest, socio-economic welfare, or other reasons for seeking an abortion, these factors could be included in the determination of health if their effect was to threaten a woman's health.
These explanatory notes do not provide much guidance to medical practitioners, to women seeking an abortion, or to Canadians generally as to what circum-

November 23, 1989
Government Orders
stances will allow a doctor to induce an abortion. They raise as many questions as they answer.
There are inherent risks and stresses in every pregnancy. However, modem medicine combined with the facilities available in most Canadian hospitals means that these risks and stresses can be controlled to such a degree that few Canadian women need fear lasting damage to their physical or even psychological well-being as a result of carrying a baby to term.
Indeed, as far as psychological health is concerned, there is evidence that an abortion may cause long-term negative effects. Should we expect qualified medical practitioners to deny virtually all requests for abortions under this bill if it becomes law? Is that the purpose of the bill? If a woman in robust health receives an abortion by a qualified medical practitioner under this law, should the casual observer conclude that section 287 of the Criminal Code has been violated? Is that what the government intends? Would it be the responsibility of such a casual observer to bring such a practitioner to justice for violating the Criminal Code? Just how would this be done?
Alternatively, is the provision relating to health to be interpreted as meaning that if a woman merely claims that her health will be threatened in some way by carrying the baby to term, a medical practitioner may agree to the abortion provided that performing the abortion would not, in his or her opinion, endanger her health or life?
Setting aside the difficult case of eugenics, rape and incest the claim might be that due to her "socio-economic circumstances" her health, physical, mental or psychological may be threatened, in which case the medical practitioner will be required to determine whether that was merely an excuse or a legitimate claim.
The explanatory notes provided by the government suggest that socio-economic circumstances would qualify as grounds for abortion if they threatened a woman's health. There are those who argue that socio-economic circumstances on their own would be sufficient justification for an abortion. If the government agrees with that view and intends that socio-economic circumstances be grounds for an abortion, this should be clearly specified in the bill as an additional reason for permitting an
abortion. Obviously, if that is to be the effect of the bill, I shall vote that this bill not pass this House.
I am not insensitive to the socio-economic difficulties which many women, in particular single mothers, face. These difficulties call for positive action on the part of governments. They call for progressive day care legislation to enable women to participate in the workforce without compromising the care they give to their children. They require more determined enforcement of legislation regarding child support so that fathers will contribute their share to the financial needs of children. They require education on family planning. Abortion is not a remedy. It is not a solution. This bill does not address these difficulties.
What is required is far more than simply a law to put abortion back into the Criminal Code. What is required is a comprehensive policy designed to bring down the number of abortions, whether legal or illegal, in Canada. This goal would be sought by education, by reducing the number of unwanted pregnancies, by support for adoption, by progressive workplaces with pay equity and day care programs that recognize the contribution of childbearing women, and abortion legislation is a necessary part of that program.
If we were at third reading stage, I would vote against this bill, but this is only second reading stage. I abhor the legal vacuum which has persisted in this country for almost two years. We must make an honest effort to get a good law on the statute books. It may be possible to amend this defective bill at the committee stage between second and third reading. For example, it may be possible to strike out the vague, imprecise reference to the health of the pregnant woman. I hope so, because if the defects of the bill are not corrected by the committee to which it is sent, I shall vote against the bill at third reading.

Mr. Speaker,
I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-43, an Act respecting abortion, since I am sure you will agree this is a very important and very delicate subject for Canadians and for the people in the riding of Terrebonne, which has not escaped the heat of this debate.
As you know, there has been a great deal of debate and a lot of controversy about this very important matter, which on some occasions, proved to be very divisive. All this makes for an extremely delicate and, above all,
November 23, 1989

controversial issue, depending on whether one is pro-life or pro-choice.
Mr. Speaker, despite ideological differences, recent events and especially what happened last summer have shown that as legislators we must act responsibly, show leadership and play our role as elected representatives in this House.
How do we define that role, Mr. Speaker? I think it was our duty was to introduce a bill that, while considering two main realities, would provide a legal framework that respects the individual rights and freedoms recognized in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and also considers Canadian society's interest in protecting the foetus.
Mr. Speaker, this balance is not easy to achieve. However, as the Supreme Court said in the Morgentaler decision, the rights of one party should not necessarily be exercised to the detriment of the other party. You will agree this leaves us with very little room to manoeuvre. If we really want legislation that is constitutionally acceptable, in other words, that passes the test of a legal challenge before the Supreme Court, I believe it is imperative to respect this balance and, above all, to resist the temptation to give it a pro-life or pro-choice image, which would have the effect of destroying this delicate balance.
Bill C-43 makes abortion a medical decision that a woman and a doctor make, based on health reasons, health being defined as physical, mental and psychological health.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, this bill recognizes that only the woman will make the decision to terminate her pregnancy, a decision which clearly is not easy for a woman to make. It is a very difficult decision and as for any medical procedure, this decision will be subject to a physician's diagnosis, as is now the case anyway, Mr. Speaker. Someone asking for a surgical operation or medical treatment must submit to a doctor's diagnosis.
The bill also states that abortion is a medical procedure which must be performed by a qualified medical practitioner. Personally, I am satisfied with that because it will criminalize illegal abortions, those which are performed outside the legal framework, and this can be considered protection for women.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, the foetus is also protected because the decision must be based on health reasons, not frivolous reasons or any reason at all, but on health reasons.
This new legislation will be part of the Criminal Code. This raises the whole issue of "recriminalizing" abortion. Certainly it would have been preferable not to do that, but what credibility would a law have without penalties for those who break it, in a country where Parliament can regulate abortion at the national level only through the Criminal Code! Let us make it clear that abortion is not being made a crime to the detriment or on the backs of women; rather, physicians will have to comply with the law.
In my opinion, it would have been preferable not to legislate in this area, but Canadian society does not see it this way and we are here to represent all the Canadian people.
This bill is not intended to, and will not, change the personal opinions of one and all, nor will it change deep convictions, people's moral convictions, whether for or against abortion.
The day after this law takes effect, Mr. Speaker, those who are deeply pro-life will remain pro-life and those who are deeply pro-choice will remain pro-choice. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I would be completely opposed to a law that would impose one set of moral values instead of another or to the detriment of another. Who am I, Mr. Speaker, to say that a woman who wants her rights respected is wrong? Or that someone who attaches very great value to the life of the foetus is not right?
When I was elected to Parliament, Mr. Speaker, it was not to become unduly involved in the personal moral values of my constituents and people in general. It was certainly not to impose anything on anybody in that regard, especially not my own point of view.
This issue touches on the deepest moral convictions of each and every one of us and I am not here to play the role of a religious leader, which I would refuse to do in any case. My role as a member of a legislative body is to put in place a balanced legislative framework which will avoid unnecessary suffering and I intend to play this role fully, Mr. Speaker.
I must tell those who would be tempted to use legislation to reduce the number of abortions in Canada and to use it restrictively to limit access to abortion that they are wrong. Never will we achieve that result with a law on abortion. All we need do is implement a coherent

Government Orders
family policy, enhance the role of mother and father, urge Canadians to acknowledge that the birth of a child has tremendous social value, and then I am sure that fewer women will opt for the ultimate resort-abortion.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, restrictive legislation would amount to nothing more than a temporary way out. Just as the old act was thrown out by the court, a more restrictive piece of legislation would probably suffer the same fate for the same reasons. So it is imperative that we understand that any abortion which might upset the balance of the Bill would be utterly unacceptable. People must be told that any amendment designed to prevent a woman from securing an abortion would fly in the face of her rights under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We would have the impression that the law is in the statute books, but the minute it would be challenged before the Supreme Court, it too would be invalidated, just as the preceding legislation was.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must confess that the abortion issue was a thorn in my side during the last election campaign, and I have found it very difficult to deal with this matter ever since I was first elected to this House. Why? In all likelihood because when I considered the question I was biased by my personal convictions. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have grown to appreciate the fact that my role here, as I said before, is not to impose any concept or moral value on anybody. Our role is to see things just as they are within the context of the Canadian people and to set up a legal structure which can be accepted and which will do away with the kind of difficult and dramatic situation women have to live through, as we saw last summer.
I received a lot of comments, advice and mail from my constituents on the subject of abortion. However complex the whole issue may be, I feel that the Bill under consideration strikes a proper balance and as Member for the riding of Terrebonne, Mr. Speaker, I intend to give this measure my full support.

As
a Member of this House who is both a woman and the mother of four children, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is important for me to deal with this new abortion bill which, by failing to take a positive stand in an effort to
please everybody, settles nothing and creates a new problem.
Abortion was liberalized in January 1988, when the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that under the Criminal Code, anybody who compels a woman to carry a foetus to term is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to legal proceedings. In spite of this decision, women are still faced with the same difficulties when they try to obtain adequate care for the purpose of terminating their pregnancies. The whole approach varies from one province to the next. In some regions, the woman who manages to secure the assistance of a physician for this purpose is considered something of a phenomenon.
In my view, it is clear that in an ideal society with its long term assistance and support services and its really efficient educative and preventive programs an abortion policy would no longer be required. Unfortunately, this is not the case. Far from it! We are still very much afraid of what the neighbours will think, we live under constant social pressure, and we are concerned with the individual freedom to make a difficult choice and to live with it. If we really want to encourage women to carry their pregnancy to term, we can do it in a practical way. We can make sure that they have easy access to adequate, abundant and affordable day care services, that they are entitled to maternity leave and decent subsidized housing, that they get legal assistance in cases of incest and family violence and that they are assured of automatic alimony payments. In short, Mr. Speaker, we should provide women with the support they need to care for their children, especially in a way which is equitable for all.

Unfortunately, the bill presented by the government does not even attempt to address the issue of alternative services. Instead of threatening women and their doctors with the heavy hand of the law, the government should have instituted programs that would provide women with real alternatives. Support systems must be in place to assist women who chose not to have abortions. The government must improve the state of child care in this country. It must address the issues of teenage pregnancy, and it must realize the gamut of complex social, religious and economic influences which play an important role in a woman's decision. It must address the inherent discrimination in this legislation that biases the availability
November 23, 1989

Government Orders
of abortion services to those women who have both the time and the money to find them.

If we really want to improve the current situation, Mr. Speaker, I suggest it is vital that men should be made fully conscious of their sexual activities and the consequences of their actions. Parents should teach their boys to take the necessary precautions not to make girls pregnant if they do not want to be responsible for their abortions. They should teach their children generally that they must live with the consequences of their actions and choices. They will be able to achieve this goal through communication and dialogue before any harm is done. Support services simply do not exist.
In our society, Mr. Speaker, it is important that all children receive adequate sex education, and have access to and use of good birth control methods. The media also have a role to play to eliminate taboos and the obsessive fear that, by talking about prevention and encouraging people to use condoms, birth-control pills or other means of contraception, we are inciting young people to have sex prematurely. I think we must stop burying our heads in the sand or turning the other way if we want to prevent unwanted pregnancies.
Any woman who has gone through an abortion can tell you that it is a difficult choice to make, a major reassessment and a permanent scar in your life. Whatever the motive behind the decision, since it is the woman who is ultimately responsible for having her pregnancy terminated and who must live with the consequences, it is important that she receive adequate care.

When a woman discovers that she is carrying an unplanned child she must face the decision herself as to what course of action she will take. If she is young, poor and has few employment opportunities, she must decide whether she wants to bring a new bom child into that situation. She must decide whether to bring a child into a cycle of poverty and deprivation, or to delay parenthood until she will be able to provide a proper environment for herself and her children. Because of the lack of support structures within this legislation there is less motivation for a woman to keep or to take her pregnancy to term.
The fact that this government has backed down on its commitment to the establishment of a national child care program does nothing to discourage the option of abortion. If day care services were accessible to all Canadian mothers, then the ability to continue working and to provide for a family would weigh the question of abortion in favour of carrying the pregnancy to term. Without such services, can our society expect a woman to automatically give up her right to choose?
The rolling back of transfer payments to the provinces for education and health care services will further limit the accessibility of abortion services if needed. Once again, poor women will be forced to use inadequate and, at times, dangerous methods because they are unable to pay for proper medical services because of the lack of provincial funding or lack of access.
It is evident that the bill before us puts a burden on doctors in Canada. If doctors become liable for a criminal act, many may simply not want to take the risk of prosecution. Already, the president of the Alberta Medical Association has warned that doctors in that province would stop performing abortions, perhaps even where necessary, in order to avoid criminal prosecution under the proposed law. This is further evidence that this bill could eliminate those services in certain areas of our country.
If we accept the proposed legislation as is then the decision as to whether a woman should have an abortion should be made between her and her doctor and not by lawyers, judges or the Government of Canada. Physicians might not want to endure the possibility of harassing techniques from various groups and could eventually not offer the services rather than risk the chance of criminal sanctions. In the end, the women of Canada are the ones who will suffer.

Mr. Speaker, a bill such as this one makes the physician responsible for the decision. Many will desist to avoid social pressure and the risk of being sued. Let us not open the door to illegal abortions which will carry consequences such as infertility, shame, rejection and a

November 23, 1989
Government Orders
return to the past in a society trying to look forward to the 21st century.

I will probably vote for this bill at second reading, but unless there are amendments there is no way that I could support it on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, when I first came here in 1984, I never thought I would have to legislate on the life or death of an unborn being. I am the father of three children, and neither my wife nor I would ever have thought that we would have to make a decision on abortion, and had we been faced with that choice, it would have really been traumatic to think that one of our children would not have an opportunity to be bom.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, an abortion is a criminal act, because I view abortion as a band-aid solution. Abortion will not solve the problem in our society. Before legislating on such an important matter, we should first ask ourselves: what causes women to seek an abortion? Why do they have to do such a thing to free themselves of an unwanted pregnancy or birth.
I think we should look at family problems, and in that respect my view is that governments have not done enough to help divorced mothers, single mothers, widows who some day are faced with a pregnancy that is unwanted for lack not necessarily of love but rather money.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, nobody up till now has thought of introducing support projects or programs helping them bring their pregnancy to term and then raise their children until such time as they can look after themselves.
This is a societal not a legislative problem, it is not a government problem. It is my view that, through the legislation now before us-after the Daigle-Tremblay saga which, as you know, Mr. Speaker, dealt with a lovers' problem by making society, or Canadians pay- this government said there was a legislative vacuum and that vacuum had to be filled. It tabled Bill C-43, which was a way of sitting on the fence.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill is pro-life with pro-choice contents. If you look at it closely you will realize immediately that it criminalizes the act and yet does not provide sufficient protection for the child to be bom, the foetus. I am convinced that we will never build a healthy and strong society if we destroy embryos. We simply cannot build something unless we begin somewhere.
Mr. Speaker, some people may suggest that the embryo or the foetus is not a living being, but keep in mind that if it is not a living being, if it is not a human being who will live, it is at least the beginning of a human being who will go on to live. It will become a human being after the gestation period. By denying that it can become a human being we deny as well that there is a beginning. If we do not acknowledge the beginning, we will destroy it. As a society, as individuals, Mr. Speaker, can we allow ourselves to destroy the beginning?
The second part of the Bill under consideration does not acknowledge or protect that, and this is why we in the House find it so difficult to state unequivocally whether we are for or against the Bill. Because on either side of the issue it answers a question we are asking. Well, I ask myself that question. Criminalizing the act because killing an unborn child has to be as close as you can get to a criminal deed, I agree and I can live with that, but the one thing I cannot live with, Mr. Speaker, is our failure to give full protection to the unborn child.
Still I must say that the bill is a step in the right direction. Perhaps it will pave the way for other laws, and perhaps we may be able to redress the situation by moving amendments once the bill reaches the committee stage.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have not used up all my allotted time before the lunch hour. May I have a few minutes after lunch to conclude my remarks?

The hon. member will have three minutes left to complete his speech when we return.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the serious subject of abortion and a piece of legislation that is before us in the House. I want it recorded that I do not stand for Bill C-43, but I will not stand against it at second reading. As I have told my constituents, I am most uncomfortable with this bill because I cannot condone the act of abortion. I cannot accept the taking of an innocent unborn.
Although C-43 does not sit well with me, I believe strongly that we in this place are obligated not to reject this bill at the outset but consider and debate its contents. We owe it to our public who sent us here and to the future generations to work diligently over the next few months on this bill, to work together as Canadians and to arrive at a position that allows eveiy one of us to sleep at night.
Mr. and Mrs. Dennis Parish of New Liskeard have asked me: "Please stand for and vote for the strictest law regarding abortion. Please make sure there are no undefined terms in it which would provide loopholes." To them, and to my constituents, I understand and I intend to do just that.

Mr. Speaker, with the completion of its first free elections, Namibia is proceeding along the path to independence.
Unfortunately, independence carries with it a financial cost. Namibia must find international support to make up for the withdrawal of budgetary support from south Africa.
Canada's long-time commitment to the well-being of Namibia cannot be abandoned now. With this government's slashing of foreign aid budgets, CIDA has been forced to cut proposed aid to Namibia by 50 per cent.
I call on the government to put its money where its mouth is, restore full funding assistance and a major package of bilateral aid to Namibia, and ensure through its position on the Security Council that Walvis Bay, Namibia's only deep water port, is removed from South African to Namibian control. Last, we must establish a high commission in Namibia or, minimally, an aid commission to Namibia.
Namibia's emergence is a forerunner of future developments in South Africa. The progress of this new nation will be watched intensely by all forces involved in southern Africa. It must not be allowed to fail.

Mr. Speaker, the FMLN in El Salvador have today called for a cease-fire in the war. Their recent dramatic escalation of that war was in response to increased government repression and violence.
The UN Commission on Human Rights in its report on El Salvador noted a dramatic increase in the number of human rights violations since the coming to power of the Arena government of President Cristiani.
The FMLN has appealed for a UN monitored ceasefire. A lasting peace is possible through sincere negotiations between the Salvadoran government and the FMLN and a reversal of current U.S. policy. Only when the United States abandons its cold war posture in the region will the people of Central America be able to exercise their sovereign right to determine their own destiny.
I once again appeal to our government to impress upon the United States that the world is changing and that the U.S. military interference in Central America is unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, my colleagues on both sides of the House paid a final tribute to my friend Jean-Claude Malepart. Since I

November 23, 1989
was in Montreal with his family, I could not pay tribute to him in this House.

Pierre Trudeau once said when MPs are 50 yards from Parliament Hill, they are no longer honourable members, they are just nobodies. Well, Trudeau would have been wrong again if he had said that about Jean Claude Malepart.

Mr. Speaker, more than 4,000 people went to pay their respects one last time over the weekend in Montreal and more than 2,000 people gathered in St. Anselm's Church to honour him in a simple and moving ceremony.
His last speech on Meech Lake in this House attracted much attention. It is no doubt what Jean-Claude Malepart leaves to all Canadians. He saw his death coming, knew that he would die and gave us his parting words. Jean-Claude Malepart, a worker for ordinary people, the Maurice Richard of politics, is now in his final resting place but lives in the hearts of many.
Mr. Speaker, cancer knocked him out, but like a great heavyweight, he continued to fight while going down. We have lost a giant defender of the people, a man with a great heart, and we will miss him for a long time.
Jean-Claude, your friend who pumps gas salutes you.

Mr. Speaker, each week when I return home to my riding, I am faced with yet another example of how detrimental the GST will be to the constituents of Malpeque.
Most recently, the reality of the proposed 9 per cent tax has hit our figure skating clubs and minor hockey clubs. These organizations represent a major part of community life in my district and indeed across Canada.
The importance of sport in young people's lives cannot be denied. Through the minor hockey clubs and the skating clubs, they experience the rewards of dedication, the importance of good sportsmanship and the benefits of physical activity.
The GST proposes to tax areas of sports programs which were previously untaxed: coaching fees, facilities, test fees, membership fees and travel costs. The effect of the GST on these items will create a financial burden that many young people and their families simply cannot afford.
On behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada and more particularly my Liberal colleagues in the House of Commons, I urge this government to keep the community spirit alive in Canada by promoting sport for youth instead of prohibiting participation with the GST.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every day more species of plants and animals come in danger of extinction, largely the impact of humans on nature.
One species, the African elephant, is now receiving the protection it needs. Commercial trade in ivory has been banned by Canada and most other nations under the Convention on the International Trade in Endangered Species. Last Friday hundreds of Canadians who care about this attended a meeting at the University of Toronto organized by Zoocheck Canada. They heard Doctor Richard Leakey, Ian and Oria Douglas-Hamilton and others speak about the plight of Africa's elephants. Over $120,000 was raised for the Kenya Wild Elephant Fund.
Concern for endangered species here in Canada and around the world measures how attentive we humans are to others with whom we share this planet and upon whom we depend for our own life and well-being.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, the Lebanese President was killed in a bombing incident. His death came not only as a shock but as a severe disappointment to the many who saw him as Lebanon's hope for peace. Around the world religious ceremonies were held to mourn this great loss.
November 23, 1989



I hope that President Mouawad's death will not lead to further bloodshed, but instead that it will bring together the citizens of that country as they mourn the death of a leader eager to restore peace to Lebanon.

It is ironic that a man so driven toward restoring peace was killed by such a brutal act of terrorism. After only 17 days in office, President Muawad was already carving out a path that could have led to peace in Lebanon. I am confident that the people of Lebanon will overcome this tragedy and hope they will follow in the late president's footsteps by continuing his efforts toward achieving a sovereign, independent, just and fair Lebanon.

Mr. Speaker, an article by journalist Jean-Denis Girouard that appeared in today's Journal de Montreal is entitled: "Housing: Quebec does not have its fair share".
Quebec is the only province that has put in place a joint cost-sharing renovation program with the federal government.
The city of Montreal's contribution was practically equal to that of Quebec and of the federal government, and over half the 6,490 renovated units were in rooming houses for the poor.
Mr. Speaker, in this situation, the cut in the rental RRAP is completely inappropriate given not only the costs but also the urgent needs of people in Quebec and Montreal, and I would ask the Minister of State (Housing) to reintroduce this program as soon as possible for the sake of Quebec's poor.

Mr. Speaker, there are those in this House and outside it who would paint the abortion issue as simply a woman's issue. Nothing could be further from the truth. It most definitely is a woman's issue in so far as it is women who are most
profoundly, indeed exclusively affected. It is a woman's issue in so far as it is women's fundamental constitutional right to security of the person that those who would deny women access to abortion propose to violate.
For this very reason, abortion is an issue of human rights that far outstrips mere gender. And it is for this veiy reason that there appears in today's The Globe and Mail an advertisement from a group called Men for Women's Choice. Endorsed by over 600 men named in the advertisement, it makes the simple and utterly fundamental statement that "no government should be able to force a woman to bear a child against her will".
These men, and the millions of other men across Canada who support and share their views, are a welcome contingent in the struggle for freedom of choice on abortion in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the New Brunswick economy has benefited greatly since this government came to power in 1984. Since 1984, over 38,000 new jobs have been created in New Brunswick alone while the number of people living below the poverty line has fallen by 26,000 over the same period.
The unemployment rate in New Brunswick has fallen from 16.3 per cent to 12.3 per cent since September 1984. Housing starts for the first five months of 1989 are up by 104 per cent from the same period in 1984. Exports increased by over one-third in 1988 as compared to 1984.
I know those opposite find it veiy difficult to listen to these very impressive figures, but I am sure the opposition members realize that we are doing a good job and will continue to do a good job in Atlantic Canada and in my home province of New Brunswick.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of this House a disturbing incident which casts in a very poor light this government's dedication to the cause of native rights and dignity in Canada.

A slide presentation on the Fathers of Confederation prepared by Parks Canada and shown to visitors to Province House in Prince Edward Island contains a reference to Canada's native peoples as heathens and infidels.
It is true that this remark is part of a contemporary quote, however the context is not made clear to viewers, who receive the impression that this is how our society regards native people. As well, the rich contribution made to our nation by Canada's original inhabitants is neglected in the presentation.
Prince Edward Islanders are shocked at the callousness and arrogance of the presentation and disturbed by the government's apparent disregard for the dignity of native people. I call upon the government to take appropriate action regarding this matter and promise all Canadians that such an incident will not be repeated.

Mr. Speaker, what is the difference between the Liberal party and the NDP? In a September 1989 speech to the Canadian Association for Securities and Studies Conference, the hon. Liberal from York Centre stated, and I quote:
It is in the nature of the Canadian opposition tradition to be irresponsible or non-responsible and I mean that in the highest sense of the word.
